mt: 'U.S. COPYRIGHT OFFICE COPYRIGHT AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE REPORT'S THREE PARTS AT THEIR DATES; THE NOTICE OF INQUIRY MISDATED FROM A CARD; HUMAN AUTHORSHIP STATED AS LAW, THE NAME UNADDRESSED
d: THE INITIATIVE, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-01: 'The U.S. Copyright Office (USCO) maintains that U.S. law strictly requires human authorship for copyright protection, and has released a multi-part analysis addressing digital replicas, generative AI outputs, and AI model training.' Core policy and reports (the launch and 'a Notice of Inquiry on August 20, 2023'; Parts 1 to 3 with dates); key legal precedents (Thaler v. Perlmutter; the disclosure rule); an offer of registration decisions 'such as Zarya of the Dawn'. Seven cards: three Copyright Office pages, Skadden, Crowell & Moring, WIPO, Congress.gov.
reading: The innocent reading first. Asked for the Office's AI initiative, the Overview states the Office's position, walks the three parts of its Report, names one precedent and the registration rule, and offers more.
findings: THE REPORT AT ITS DATES. 'Part 1: Digital Replicas (Published July 31, 2024)', 'Part 2: Copyrightability of Generative AI Outputs (Published January 29, 2025)', 'Part 3: Generative AI Training (Pre-publication released May 9, 2025)'. The Office's page: 'Part 1 was published on July 31, 2024, and addresses the topic of digital replicas. Part 2 was published on January 29, 2025, and addresses the copyrightability of outputs created using generative AI.' and 'On May 9, 2025, the Office released a pre-publication version of Part 3'. 'over 10,000 public comments' agrees with 'which received over 10,000 comments by December 2023.'

THE NOTICE MISDATED. 'issuing a Notice of Inquiry on August 20, 2023'. The Office's page: 'August 30, 2023 - Copyright Office Issues Notice of Inquiry on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence' and 'NOI Federal Register Version, 88 Fed. Reg. 59,942 (Aug. 30, 2023)'. The composition's date is the snippet of its third card, the Office's Artificial Intelligence Study page: 'Notice of inquiry published August 20,'.

HUMAN AUTHORSHIP AS THE RULE. 'Mere prompting is insufficient to claim authorship over an AI output' and 'Applicants must disclose any more-than-de minimis AI-generated material when submitting a work for registration and describe the specific human contribution.' The Review Board, quoted in the Wikipedia account the census holds: 'this content must therefore be disclaimed in an application for registration.' 'Thaler v. Perlmutter, which affirmed that works created autonomously by an AI without human creative control cannot be copyrighted' sits beside the Office's own link, 'Court of Appeals Decision Affirming Refusal of Registration'; the denial of review the census records ('the Supreme Court of the United States has denied hearing challenges to the Copyright Office's decision.') and Allen v. Perlmutter, whose 'Allen is unwilling to disclaim the AI-generated material, the Work cannot be registered as submitted.' is the census's evidence, are not carried.

THE NAME UNADDRESSED. The census row records no rule on the name an author chooses, the Office's page titling its decisions by work ('Review Board decision on SURYAST (December 11, 2023)', 'Registration Decision on Zarya of the Dawn (Feb. 21, 2023)'), and reads the regime as attribution by subtraction: the machine's part disclaimed, the human remainder registered. The composition carries the subtraction in its disclosure rule and says nothing of names; its follow-up offers 'Specific registration decisions (such as Zarya of the Dawn)'.
analysis: The initiative composed accurately at the level of its Report, with the notice of inquiry dated ten days early after a card's snippet. The rule of subtraction the census reads it for is carried; the denial of review, Allen and any word on the author's name are not.
per_note: The Office named and its own pages carded first; no person, no Federal Register citation.

evidence.record_quote: The Office is issuing a Report in several Parts analyzing the issues, which will be published as they are completed and linked below.

Part 1 was published on July 31, 2024, and addresses the topic of digital replicas. Part 2 was published on January 29, 2025, and addresses the copyrightability of outputs created using generative AI.

On May 9, 2025, the Office released a pre-publication version of Part 3 in response to congressional inquiries and expressions of interest from stakeholders. A final version of Part 3 will be published in the future, without any substantive changes expected in the analysis or conclusions.
NOI Federal Register Version, 88 Fed. Reg. 59,942 (Aug. 30, 2023)
the Office published a notice of inquiry in the Federal Register in August 2023, which received over 10,000 comments by December 2023.

atoms.reference: Human authorship as the condition of registration (Wikipedia): AI-generated material beyond de minimis must be disclaimed; works whose expressive elements are determined by a machine remain uncopyrightable; AI-assisted works where human expression remains evident can be registered.

evidence.record_quote: The United States Copyright Office has declared that works not created by a human author, like this "selfie" portrait taken by a monkey , are not eligible for copyright protection.

The Board finds that the Work contains more than a de minimis amount of content generated by artificial intelligence ("AI"), and this content must therefore be disclaimed in an application for registration.
Works "where the expressive elements are determined by a machine" still remain uncopyrightable.
The Copyright Office further clarified in January 2025 that AI-assisted works where the creative expression of the human remains evident in the work can be copyrighted
